The most funded industry in human history just got told it is solving the wrong problem, by one of its own pioneers. LeCun: "Babies learn this around the age of eight or nine months, that objects don't float, they fall." No training data. No labels. No reward function. A nine month old tosses a spoon off a high chair and encodes a physics engine no model on Earth can match. LeCun: "Most of us can learn to drive in about 20 or 30 hours of training without ever crashing, causing any accident." Thirty hours at most. Tesla has spent billions of miles building the most advanced driving system on public roads. A sixteen year old gets there across a weekend. Not because teenagers are superior drivers. Because they are not learning to drive from scratch. They are deploying a world model built across sixteen years of living. LeCun: "If we drive next to a cliff, we know that if we turn the wheel to the right, the car is going to run off the cliff and nothing good is going to come out of this." You run the mental simulation. You see the fall. You sense what comes next. You keep the wheel straight. None of it was real. All of it counted as intelligence. An AI must fail a thousand times to internalize what you worked out in your head without moving. That is not a capability gap. That is an architecture gap. LeCun: "The main problem we need to solve is how do we learn models of the world." Not larger models. Not more compute. Not another trillion tokens consumed. World models. Systems that can project forward through reality before taking a single action. The whole industry is racing to scale language. LeCun argues language is a compression of thought. Not thought itself. You knew gravity before you ever owned the word for it. You understood cause and effect long before your first full sentence. The most sophisticated intelligence you will ever have was assembled in total silence. And every AI lab alive is trying to reconstruct thinking from text alone. Physics does not care about your context window. A baby who learns cups fall at home already understands that rocks fall from clifftops. No retraining. No fine-tuning. One model. Every environment. That is what real intelligence looks like. Not prediction. Not pattern matching. Not scale. A simulation of reality detailed enough to rehearse futures that never happened. How to Set Up Projects in Claude Turn conversations into compounding assets. Projects in Claude are your persistent memory layer. Why use projects: memory keeps context, files, and decisions across sessions. Workspace organizes knowledge, assets, and deliverables in one dedicated space. Execution via Cowork lets you collaborate on multi-step, long-running tasks. Scoped context focuses Claude's attention on what matters for this specific work. 5 steps to set up a project: create a project by heading to Claude Projects and starting a new one. Add instructions, a project brief with goals, rules, and how Claude should work. Add context, attaching relevant files, docs, and references to ground the project. Run work, start a conversation and let Claude get to work with full project context. Stack with skills, adding capabilities Claude can call on demand. Projects vs Skills: projects are containers, skills are capabilities, projects hold your work while skills power how Claude does it. Projects store context, skills store expertise. Use projects for what you're building, skills for how Claude should think, write, analyze, or act. Stack them together, projects provide the context, skills provide the capabilities, that's where the magic happens. Suggested folder convention: /reference, /analysis, /deliverables. Claude's context stack, top to bottom: global memory (account-level), context files (user-provided), project instructions & files (specific to this project), skills (reusable capabilities), and your current prompt. An analysis of 129,000 websites, 216,524 pages and 100,000 prompts determined the #1 secret to getting traffic from ChatGPT. It busts a lot of myths and lines up closely with what we’ve learned about how AI search systems retrieve, evaluate and reuse information. It also aligns with what SEO Stuff has been building over the past year: https://seo-stuff.com Let’s break it down. Headline first: backlinks mattered more than anything else. The SE Ranking study found that sites with 32,000+ referring domains were 3.5x more likely to be cited by ChatGPT. Sites with very high domain trust also earned nearly 4x more citations than low-trust domains. If you want to see where your site stands across Google and AI search, start here. It’s free: https://seo-stuff.com/free-audit ChatGPT may ignore some old-school SEO tricks, but authority clearly matters. High-authority domains are more likely to rank, get discovered, enter AI retrieval and ultimately get cited. That is why SEO Stuff's flagship package includes three contextually relevant DR50+ backlinks: https://seo-stuff.com/gold-plan-package Homepage traffic was another major signal. Sites with 7,900+ homepage visitors had twice the citation likelihood, while domains with 190,000+ monthly visitors earned nearly twice as many citations as smaller sites. That reinforces something important. AI search does not exist in isolation from traditional search visibility. If your domain has almost no presence across the wider search ecosystem, it has fewer opportunities to enter AI retrieval in the first place. This is why SEO Stuff content is built for Google and LLMs at the same time. Presence on Quora and Reddit mattered too. Domains with a lot of Quora and Reddit mentions had four times higher citation likelihood. Even smaller brands saw measurable lifts from participating in relevant discussions and being referenced organically. Those mentions can reinforce what the company does, which category it belongs to and whether real people are talking about it. Content depth also mattered. Articles under 800 words averaged 3.2 citations, while articles over 2,900 words averaged 5.1, but simply adding words is not enough. The stronger content included multiple angles, examples, expert quotes, verifiable data and broader topic coverage. That is the thinking behind the Premium Content Bundle: https://seo-stuff.com/premium-content-bundle-service It includes 60 long-form articles designed to build deeper coverage around the questions customers and AI systems are researching. Structure made a major difference too. Well-structured pages earned 70% more citations. The strongest pages used clean headings, relatively concise sections, logical progression, question-based H2s and clear answers. Walls of text and vague brand storytelling give LLMs much less they can reliably extract. Freshness mattered as well. Pages updated within the previous three months nearly doubled their citations, with older pages averaging 3.6 citations compared with 6.0 for recently updated content. Newer does not automatically mean better, but keeping important pages current clearly matters. Question-based titles and FAQs also helped, particularly for smaller sites, when combined with depth, authority and good structure. LLMs.txt, on the other hand, did almost nothing. Its impact was negligible. Authority, structure and useful content mattered far more. Review platforms were another strong signal. Brands appearing on Trustpilot, Capterra, G2, Sitejabber and Yelp earned three to six times more citations than brands with no presence. That is another reminder that AI systems do not evaluate your company only through your own website. Third-party reputation matters. Core Web Vitals mattered too. Fast pages were cited three times more often than slow pages. You do not need perfect scores, but you do need to avoid a site that is painfully slow or difficult to use. So what actually drives ChatGPT visibility? The study points to backlinks, domain trust, homepage authority, Reddit and Quora presence, deep content, clear structure, recent updates, review platform visibility and fast performance. In other words, many of the fundamentals that help you in Google also help you in AI search, with additional social, structural and entity signals layered on top. Define these four things for every AI agent before it exists and the workflow holds up in production. Skipping the planning step is the fastest way to end up with an agent team that breaks on contact with real work. Map the workflow first. Write down every step from the incoming request to the delivered result, in order, before any building starts. Then write the four definitions for every agent in the chain. Its input names what it receives to start the job. Its trigger names what kicks it off, whether a form submission, an incoming email, a schedule, or a CRM update. Its actions name what it does with the input. Its expected output names what it hands forward, described precisely enough to check. Build the agents one at a time and test each one alone before connecting anything. A broken agent inside a connected workflow hides behind the others, while a broken agent in isolation shows you exactly what failed. Connect the chain only after every agent passes on its own, then run the complete workflow end to end. The work continues after launch. Check the logs regularly and refine the prompts, instructions, and logic as real outputs show you where the weak spots sit. No-code platforms handle the wiring, so none of this requires programming. PwC's mid-2026 outlook calls what's happening to software deals a "SaaS-pocalypse." A SaaS company charging $50/seat/month for workflow automation was worth 8-12x revenue when buyers believed switching costs would protect that revenue for five to seven years. Then an AI agent showed up that does 80% of the same work for $200/month flat, no annual contract, no six-month implementation. Once buyers saw the alternative, they stopped paying the premium. I sat across from a PE operating partner last quarter evaluating a compliance software acquisition. ARR looked strong, net retention above 110%. Traditional diligence said buy. We opened the product. The core workflow ran on hardcoded decision trees with no learning loop and no defensible technical layer. Two engineers with Claude and eight weeks could rebuild it. He killed the deal. The moat was gone. The diligence question used to be "does this company use AI?" Now it's "can AI replace this company's product?" I keep seeing two patterns across the portfolio companies we assess. Companies that bolted AI onto existing products. They added a chatbot to the support page and put "AI-powered" on the website, but the core product architecture didn't change. These companies face the most risk because the AI is cosmetic and the underlying product is replaceable. Companies that rebuilt around AI. They trained models on proprietary data and built feedback loops that compound domain knowledge with each customer interaction. Their moat gets deeper every month they operate. PwC's data confirms the split. Fundraising dollars rose 9% in H1 2026 even though fewer funds closed. Top managers, the ones who can tell which portfolio companies fall in group two, raised capital fast. The rest sat through skeptical investor committees and extended timelines. We've done enough pre-acquisition technical assessments to know the tells: thin-wrapper architecture and model pipelines that live in one engineer's head. Those tells separate a defensible AI company from one that happens to call an API. Healthcare has been the most resilient PE sector this year, with financial services and compliance close behind. All three share one characteristic: compliance requirements make it harder for generic AI to compete without domain-specific engineering. That's where we spend most of our time.
